exampleAnswers.title: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

question.text: Given that $a \equiv b \, (\textrm{mod}\,17),$ construct a statement that also must be true:
question.explanation:
The subtraction property states that

\[ a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

\[ a \equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a - \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}5} \equiv b - \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}5} \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,17) \]

example.title: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $x +5 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15)?$
question.explanation:
The addition property of congruences states that

\[ a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

\[ a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

\begin{align*} x +5 & \equiv 11 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,15) \\[3pt] x +5 - 5 & \equiv 11 - 5 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,15) \\[3pt] x & \equiv 6 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,15) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N

question.text: Which of the following is congruent to $0$ modulo $14?$
question.explanation:
First, recall that

\[ a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn, \]

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $14$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $14.$

Therefore, since $14\,|\,(-84),$ we obtain

\[ -84 \equiv (-6) \cdot {\color{blue}14} \equiv (-6)\cdot 0 \equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}14}). \] None of the other options are multiples of $14.$

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $x \equiv 7\: (\textrm{mod}\,12)?$
question.explanation:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that ${\color{blue}12} \cdot 2 \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}12})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

\begin{align*} x + 0 & \equiv 7+0 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,12) \\[3pt] x & \equiv 7+0 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,12) \\[3pt] & \equiv 7+{\color{blue}12}\cdot 2 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,{\color{blue}12}) \\[3pt] &\equiv 7+24 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,12) \\[3pt] &\equiv 31 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,12) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Simplifying Congruences

question.text:
The United States Declaration of Independence was ratified on July 4th, 1776. Given that January 1st, 1776, was a Monday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week the Declaration of Independence was ratified.

Hint: The year 1776 was a leap year since it's divisible by $4$ and is not an end-of-century year.
question.explanation:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1776, and July 1st, 1776.

  • There were $3$ months with $31$ days (January, March, and May).

  • There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April, and June).

  • There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and July 4th is given by \[ d = \overbrace{31(3) + 30(2) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to July 1st}} + 3. \]

Now, note that \[ 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1, \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7). \]

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} d &=3(31) + 2(30) + 1(29) + 3 \\[5pt] &\equiv 3(3) + 2(2) + 1(1) + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 9 + 4 + 1 + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 2 + 4 + 1 + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 10 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $3$ days after January 1st, 1776, namely Thursday.

example.title: Date Problems

question.text:
On November 16th, 1700, Spain's King Charles II died. Given that January 1st, 1700, was a Friday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week Charles II died.

Hint: The year 1700 was not a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and is not divisible by $400.$
question.explanation:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1700, and November 1st, 1700.

  • There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

  • There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

  • There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 16th is given by \[ d = \overbrace{31(6) + 30(3) + 28(1)}^{\textrm{days to November 1st}} + 15. \]

Now, note that \[ 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 28\equiv 0, \qquad 15\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7). \]

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} d &=6(31) + 3(30) + 1(28) + 15 \\[5pt] &\equiv 6(3) + 3(2) + (0) + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 18 + 6 + 0 + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 4 + 6 + 0 + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 11 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 4 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $4$ days after January 1st, 1700, namely Tuesday.

example.title: Date Problems

question.text:
The famous mathematician Alan Turing was born on June 23rd, 1912. Given that January 1st, 1912, was a Monday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week Alan Turing was born.

Hint: The year 1912 was a leap year since it's divisible by $4$ and is not an end-of-century year.
question.explanation:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1912, and June 1st, 1912.

  • There were $3$ months with $31$ days (January, March, and May).

  • There was $1$ month with $30$ days (April).

  • There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and June 23rd is given by \[ d = \overbrace{31(3) + 30(1) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to June 1st}} + 22. \]

Now, note that \[ 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1, \qquad 22\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7). \]

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} d &=3(31) + 1(30) + 1(29) + 22 \\[5pt] &\equiv 3(3) + 1(2) + 1(1) + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 9 + 2 + 1 + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 6 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $6$ days after January 1st, 1912, namely Sunday.

example.title: Date Problems

question.text:
Jacopo Peri's Euridice, modern opera's earliest known, fully surviving work, was first performed in Florence on October 6th, 1600. Given that January 1st, 1600, was a Saturday, use congruences to determine the day of the week on which the opera was first performed.

Hint: The year 1600 was a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and divisible by $400.$
question.explanation:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1600, and October 1st, 1600.

  • There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, and August).

  • There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

  • There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and October 6th is given by \[ d = \overbrace{31(5) + 30(3) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to October 1st}} + 5. \]

Now, note that \[ 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1, \qquad 5\equiv 5, \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7). \]

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} d &=5(31) + 3(30) + 1(29) + 5 \\[5pt] &\equiv 5(3) + 3(2) + (1) + 5 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 15 + 6 + 1 + 5 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 1 + 6 + 1 + 5 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 13 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 6 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date 6 days after January 1st, 1600, namely Friday.

example.title: Date Problems

question.text:
On November 11th, 1918, an armistice was signed between the Germans and the Allies, ending World War I. Given that January 1st, 1918, was a Tuesday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week the war was over.

Hint: The year 1918 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$
question.explanation:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1918, and November 1st, 1918.

  • There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

  • There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

  • There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 11th is given by \[ d = \overbrace{31(6) + 30(3) + 28(1)}^{\textrm{days to November 1st}} + 10. \]

Now, note that \[ 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 28\equiv 0, \qquad 10 \equiv 3 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7). \]

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} d &= 6(31) + 3(30) + 1(28) + 10 \\[5pt] &\equiv 6(3) + 3(2) + 1(0) + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 18 + 6 + 0 + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 4 + 6 + 0 + 3 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 13 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 6 \quad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $6$ days after January 1st, 1918, namely Monday.
